papers.title: Sampling strategies for selecting general population comparison cohorts.
papers.one_line: Compares three ways of drawing a matched general-population comparison cohort in Danish registry data and shows that sampling without replacement in random order conditions on the future, inflating outcome rates in the comparator when comparators are themselves at substantial risk.
papers.what_was_done: A matched comparison cohort drawn from linkable population registries lets a patient cohort be read against the general population, but the sampling scheme itself can create bias. Index cohorts of Danish individuals alive and free of ischemic stroke at the index date, and separately of individuals older than 50, had comparison cohorts drawn 5:1 or 1:1 by three strategies: without replacement in random order, with replacement, and without replacement in chronological order. Sampling without replacement in random order removes from the pool anyone already sampled, which uses information about the future and inflated outcome rates, though only measurably when index persons were older than 50 or the comparison cohort took a large share of the source population. Sampling without replacement in chronological order failed to find enough comparators for the older cohort and produced comparison cohorts skewed young with lower mortality. A heart failure cohort reproduced the pattern seen with age above 50. Sampling with replacement, or 1:1 matching, showed no systematic difference. The paper does not provide a way to quantify the size of the differences in general, and reports that most published studies using a general-population comparator do not state which strategy they used.

future_research.gap: No means exists of quantifying in advance how large the bias from a given comparator-sampling strategy will be in a new setting.
future_research.quote: Although it showed differences between comparison cohorts selected by different sampling strategies in some settings, it did not present means of quantifying the size of these differences in general.

future_research.gap: Differences between sampling strategies in baseline covariates beyond the matching factors were not assessed.
future_research.quote: Moreover, there might be differences between sampling strategies which we did not detect, eg, we did not assess baseline covariates beyond the matching factors.

problems.evidence: Removing an individual from the sampling pool once drawn is a rule about the whole study period applied at a single index date, so membership of the comparison cohort depends on events after time zero. The bias is the same conditioning-on-the-future mechanism that produces immortal time, arriving through the comparator construction rather than through exposure classification.
problems.quote: However, sampling without replacement in random order can lead to immortal time bias by conditioning on the future.

problems.evidence: The scheme by which the untreated comparator is drawn changes the estimate when comparators are at substantial outcome risk, and the review of published work found that most studies do not report which scheme they used. A design choice with a demonstrated effect on the result is therefore invisible to a reader.
problems.quote: While a few studies reported sampling with replacement, 5 , 19 the sampling strategy was not described in others. 6 – 18

new_problems.proposed_title: Nothing bounds the bias a general-population comparator sampling scheme introduces before the study is run
new_problems.statement: An emulation of a no-treatment arm is often built by matching each patient to comparators drawn from a population registry. Which sampling scheme is used, without replacement in random order, with replacement, or without replacement in chronological order, changes the outcome rate in the comparator arm, and the direction depends on the sampling ratio and on the comparators' own outcome risk. There is no procedure that bounds the resulting bias from quantities known before the analysis, so the scheme is chosen by convention and its consequences are read off after the fact, one dataset at a time.
new_problems.why_open: Sampling without replacement in random order makes cohort membership depend on the whole study period, which is the same conditioning-on-the-future mechanism as immortal time, and it is demonstrably consequential when comparators are at substantial outcome risk. Sampling without replacement in chronological order fails to find comparators for older patients and returns a cohort skewed young. The empirical demonstration is confined to one registry, two outcomes and one disease, and the authors state that they cannot quantify the differences in general. Published studies using this design mostly do not report the scheme, so the magnitude cannot be recovered from the literature either.
new_problems.quote: Although it showed differences between comparison cohorts selected by different sampling strategies in some settings, it did not present means of quantifying the size of these differences in general.
new_problems.checked_against_index: ELG-01 concerns eligibility criteria that the data do not record; here the criteria are recorded and the bias comes from the order in which eligible comparators are consumed. ELG-02 concerns colliders induced by healthcare-use variables in the eligibility definition, not by the sampling scheme. TZO-01 covers the time grid and grace period for the exposed strategy, not comparator construction, and the finding above is filed there only for the conditioning-on-the-future mechanism.

papers.title: Comparative performance of a modified landmark approach when no time of treatment data are available within oncological databases: exemplary cohort study among resected pancreatic cancer patients.
papers.one_line: Applies immortal-time-biased, Mantel-Byar, conventional landmark and modified landmark analyses to 5,668 resected pancreatic cancer patients in three national registries and shows the modified landmark estimate is a function of the cutoff time chosen.
papers.what_was_done: When a registry records that adjuvant chemotherapy was given but not when it started, the Mantel-Byar method cannot be applied, and a modified landmark approach assumes initiation at a predefined landmark. Data from Belgium, the Netherlands and Slovenia covering 5,668 resected pancreatic cancer patients diagnosed 2003 to 2014 with 10,921 person-years of follow-up were analyzed under each approach. Misclassifying the time to initiation gave an overall hazard ratio of 0.68 with 95 percent interval 0.62 to 0.75, against 0.82 with interval 0.71 to 0.93 under Mantel-Byar, an almost two-fold overstatement of benefit. The conventional landmark approach was conservative at 0.86 with interval 0.75 to 1.00 at 15 weeks, because a patient starting treatment after the landmark is modeled as unexposed for all of follow-up. Modified landmark estimates moved with the cutoff and matched Mantel-Byar at 15 weeks, 0.81 with interval 0.70 to 0.94, which corresponded to adding a 25 percent grace period to the initiation time suggested by randomized trials. Misclassified exposed person-time fell to 0.3 percent of total follow-up at the 15-week cutoff. Later cutoffs exclude more patients with early events, so the choice trades residual immortal time against selection and power.

future_research.gap: There is no general rule for the landmark cutoff; it has to be re-derived for each question and each disease from outside sources.
future_research.quote: Therefore, the choice of the best cutoff time has to be pre-evaluated for every specific research question and cancer entity.
future_research.locator: Discussion, limitations of the modified landmark approach

future_research.gap: No criterion balances the two errors the cutoff trades off, residual immortal time against exclusion of patients with early events.
future_research.quote: Therefore, a good balance in the choice of the landmark time has to be found, because the later a landmark cutoff time is defined, the less possible it is that “immortal” person-time is included but also that more patients will be excluded (unobserved) from the analysis.

problems.evidence: The estimate is a function of a cutoff the analyst picks, and the paper's own recommendation is to report a sequence of cutoffs rather than to derive one. The best-performing value was found by comparing against a gold standard that is unavailable in the setting where the method is needed: the 15-week cutoff was validated against Mantel-Byar estimates computed from initiation times that the target databases do not record.
problems.quote: A critical decision in conducting a modified landmark analysis is the choice of the landmark cutoff time.

problems.evidence: Time of treatment initiation is a protocol component that the data source does not carry, and the response is not a noisier version of the intended analysis but a different one: exposure is assigned at an assumed date, so some patients are modeled as exposed before they were treated. The paper states that this leaves residual bias rather than removing it.
problems.quote: This is why it is important to emphasize that the modified landmark approach only mitigates – but does not completely remove – immortal time bias, because the gap of the expected and the actual treatment initiation among some patients still leads to a small immortal time gap.

problems.evidence: Adding a 25 percent grace period to the initiation time suggested by randomized trials is the operation that made the modified landmark estimate agree with the gold standard, and it was found by trying 9, 12 and 15 weeks rather than derived from anything clinical. The grace period is thus a fitted quantity presented as a design parameter.
problems.quote: It was found that adding a 25% grace period to the cutoff time suggested by RCTs led to the best performance relative to the Mantel– Byar method.

papers.title: Immortal Time Bias in Observational Studies of Time-to-Event Outcomes: Assessing Effects of Postmastectomy Radiation Therapy Using the National Cancer Database.
papers.one_line: In 11,626 National Cancer Database women, standard Cox regression makes postmastectomy radiation look protective while time-dependent and landmark models estimate no effect, and a simulation shows landmark results move with the landmark time.
papers.what_was_done: A cohort of 11,626 women who received neoadjuvant chemotherapy and underwent mastectomy with pathologically positive nodes was drawn from the National Cancer Database for 2004 to 2008. Standard Cox regression comparing overall survival by receipt of postmastectomy radiation gave a hazard ratio of 0.93 with 95 percent interval 0.88 to 0.99, a significant benefit. Time-dependent and 12-month landmark models gave 0.97 with interval 0.92 to 1.03 and 0.98 with interval 0.92 to 1.04, no effect. A simulation with Weibull times varied the shape and scale of time-to-event and time-to-treatment and evaluated coverage and root mean squared error. Standard Cox overstated the effect whenever the mean time-to-event was of the same order as the mean time-to-treatment, and was unbiased only when the event time was much longer. Time-dependent estimates were closest to the truth. Landmark estimates depended on the landmark time: a longer landmark excluded more patients and cost power, a shorter one gave an incomplete picture when a large immediate effect was expected. The paper notes it did not consider confounders and did not evaluate the interaction with missing data or with binary outcomes.

future_research.gap: How immortal time bias behaves when the outcome is binary rather than a censored survival time is not established.
future_research.quote: More studies are required to examine whether similar statistical approaches can account for ITB when considering other types of outcomes.

future_research.gap: The interaction between immortal time bias and covariate missingness handled by multiple imputation has not been studied.
future_research.quote: Other studies will be needed to know how ITB behaves when covariates included in the models have missing data that were addressed by multiple imputation methods.

problems.evidence: The landmark estimate is reported as a function of the landmark time, with the two failure directions named but no rule given for choosing between them. The simulation makes the dependence quantitative rather than conceptual, and the paper's own analysis fixes the landmark at 12 months without a stated derivation.
problems.quote: The landmark model results were highly dependent on landmark timing.

problems.evidence: The cohort was chosen partly because it had no missing data, and the paper states that whether the same analytic choices control immortal time bias under imputation is unknown. Time-related bias and missingness are handled by separate literatures that the paper does not connect.
problems.quote: Finally, our sample had no missing data.

problems.evidence: The paper's own generalizability caveat is that its results were obtained where the outcome is a censored survival time, and it cites a study finding that treating mortality as a binary variable makes the bias more extreme and affects precision differently. The choice of outcome scale therefore changes both the size and the character of the bias, and is not analyzed.
problems.quote: For example, one study of acute pancreatitis asserted that when mortality is treated as a binary variable, ITB may be more extreme and may affect precision differently than in studies focused on other outcomes.

papers.title: The Challenges and Opportunities of Pharmacoepidemiology in Bone Diseases.
papers.one_line: Reviews the design and bias repertoire of osteoporosis pharmacoepidemiology and lists immortal time bias, time-varying confounding, missing data and residual confounding as challenges each met by naming a method rather than a criterion.
papers.what_was_done: Randomized trials establish efficacy in selected populations; observational pharmacoepidemiology aims at effects under practice conditions and is limited by data quality, completeness and confounding. The review sets out primary sources, prospectively collected data and registries, against secondary sources such as electronic medical records and administrative claims, and argues the latter buy size, representativeness and rare-event capture at low cost while losing ad hoc measurement. Cohort and case-control designs are compared on what each can estimate. Four challenges are then treated. Missing data is described as common in routine data and frequently handled by multiple imputation. Confounding by indication is attributed to the absence of randomization and met with multivariable regression and propensity score adjustment, matching, stratification, trimming or weighting. Immortal time bias, defined as a period during which a subject is artefactually event-free by study design, and time-varying confounding are both assigned to time-dependent modeling. Residual uncontrolled confounding is described as difficult to assess, with sensitivity analyses and instrumental variables offered. A worked motivation is that patients with severe chronic kidney disease were excluded from most bisphosphonate trials, so first-line therapies are contraindicated in a growing at-risk group whose risks and benefits are unknown.

future_research.gap: The risks and benefits of first-line osteoporosis therapy in severe chronic kidney disease are unknown because trials excluded these patients, and the contraindication rests on that absence.
future_research.quote: Therefore, the potential risks and benefits of those medications in this growing group of the population are unknown, and hence first‐line therapies (eg, bisphosphonates) are contraindicated in this relevant at‐risk population.

problems.evidence: Residual confounding is the last item in the list and is the one for which the review offers no assessment procedure, only a class of analyses to consider. The four challenges are treated as separable, each with its own remedy, and nothing addresses the case where several are violated at once.
problems.quote: Finally, residual “uncontrolled” confounding is difficult to assess, and hence to account for it, sensitivity analyses and specific methods (eg, instrumental variables) should be considered.

problems.evidence: Immortal time bias is defined and then discharged by naming time-dependent modeling, with no statement of how the time grid or the exposure window is to be set. The definition given, a period during which a subject is artefactually event-free by study design, locates the problem in the design without offering a design criterion.
problems.quote: In addition, immortal time bias (time period during which a subject is artefactually event‐free by study design) and time‐varying confounding (patient characteristics changing over time) are other types of biases usually accounted for using time‐dependent modeling.

problems.evidence: The confounding remedy is given as a menu, propensity score adjustment, matching, stratification, trimming or weighting, with no criterion for selecting among them and no requirement that a study demonstrate the choice did not matter. The review is aimed at practitioners and reproduces the menu as guidance.
problems.quote: Second, confounding by indication arises because of the lack of randomization; multivariable regression and more specific techniques such as propensity scores (adjustment, matching, stratification, trimming, or weighting) are used to minimize such biases.

papers.title: How to estimate the effect of treatment duration on survival outcomes using observational data.
papers.one_line: States the three-step clone, censor and weight procedure for treatment-duration strategies, and locates its validity entirely in the assumption that all time-fixed and time-varying confounders are measured and adjusted for.
papers.what_was_done: Only people who survive a long time can be treated for a long time, so a direct comparison of long-term users, short-term users and non-users of a drug is biased. Randomized trials do not have this problem because people are classified by the duration they were assigned rather than the duration they achieved, which accepts that dead people do not deviate from their assigned strategy. Transferring that insight to observational data gives three steps: clone each individual so that every strategy consistent with their data at time zero is assigned, censor each clone when its data stop being consistent with its assigned strategy, and use inverse probability weighting to remove the selection bias that artificial censoring introduces. A two-time-point worked example with a null effect, no confounding and no loss to follow-up shows the immortal time bias in the naive analysis and its absence under the procedure. The method extends to multiple time points and to any sustained strategy including dynamic ones such as increasing an epoetin dose when hemoglobin drops below 10 g/dL. Robins's g-formula is the stated alternative that also handles treatment-confounder feedback; the three-step procedure is preferred on implementability rather than on identification.

problems.evidence: Cloning at time zero removes immortal time bias by construction rather than by an analytic correction, because every strategy is assigned before any post-baseline information is used. What it does not do is fix the time grid or the grace period: the procedure takes the set of strategies as given, and the worked example uses discrete time points supplied by the analyst.
problems.quote:
Cloning is used to assign
people to treatment duration strategies at time zero,
eliminating immortal time bias.

problems.evidence: Two estimators are named for the same estimand, the three-step procedure and the g-formula, and the ground given for choosing between them is implementation effort rather than any property of the estimate. No requirement is stated that a study show its choice did not matter.
problems.quote:
Unlike the g formula,
however, the three step method can be easily
implemented using standard statistical software, even
for longitudinal data.

problems.evidence: The procedure eliminates one bias exactly and leaves the identification burden untouched, which the paper states as its own boundary: validity rests on all confounders being correctly measured and adjusted for. Nothing in the three steps diagnoses whether that holds, and the stated benefit is that researchers can now attend to the biases that are not so easily eliminated.
problems.quote:
Validity
of the observational estimates relies on the assumption
that all time fixed and time varying confounders are
correctly measured and adjusted for.

papers.title: Patients with Staged Bilateral Total Joint Arthroplasty in Registries: Immortal Time Bias and Methodological Options.
papers.one_line: Shows that splitting arthroplasty registry patients into unilateral and staged bilateral subgroups conditions on a status attained after follow-up starts, and that the resulting bias runs in opposite directions for death and for revision.
papers.what_was_done: Arthroplasty registries record around 20 percent of patients receiving a second joint during follow-up, and a common recommendation is to analyze staged bilateral patients as a separate subgroup. Because bilateral status is only known at the end of follow-up, that subgroup is defined by a characteristic not available at the start. An artificial data example shows the mechanism: patients who would have become bilateral but died first are observed as unilateral, so the cumulative incidence of death is overestimated for unilateral patients and underestimated to zero for bilateral ones, while for revision the direction reverses because the unilateral risk set is inflated by patients who would have crossed over. Cumulative incidences were computed by subgroup and by landmark analysis on Dutch Arthroplasty Register hip data and on simulations. The subgroup analysis produced more false detections of a difference than landmark analysis, and the death estimate was more affected than the revision estimate. The bias grows with the proportion of bilateral patients and with follow-up length; the Swedish register reports 23-year revision rates up to 38.5 percent. Landmark analysis prevents the bias but answers a conditional question restricted to patients alive and unrevised at the landmark; multistate models are offered for questions landmark analysis cannot answer.

future_research.gap: How to analyze registry data containing staged bilateral patients has no agreed answer.
future_research.quote: No consensus has been achieved on how to analyse these data in a methodological sound way.10

future_research.gap: Because revisions before the landmark are excluded, a landmark analysis cannot distinguish no difference between subgroups from a difference that has already resolved.
future_research.quote:
Thus, we cannot tell whether there is truly no difference between the two
subgroups, or if there is a difference that disappears before the 3 year landmark time.

problems.evidence: The landmark time is the whole content of the fix, and the paper shows both of its failure modes without giving a rule: too early and the bias survives, too late and the estimand becomes conditional on surviving unrevised to that point, with revisions before it dropped from the analysis entirely.
problems.quote:
On the other hand, the main disadvantage is that the conclusions only hold for
patients who are still alive and unrevised until the landmark time point.

problems.evidence: The bias exists only because death competes with revision: revision does not prevent a patient from becoming bilateral, so on its own there is no immortal time. The paper locates the problem precisely at the intersection of the subgroup definition and the competing risk, which is what makes handling death as a nuisance censoring event untenable here.
problems.quote: The immortal time bias lies at their intersection.

problems.evidence: One patient contributes two joints on two different clocks, and the review of options confirms that the field has no settled treatment: modeling within-patient correlation and analyzing bilaterals as a subgroup both ignore the time between surgeries, randomly picking one limb depends on the draw, and treating all joints as independent is recommended elsewhere on the grounds that it usually does not matter much.
problems.quote:
Options (i) and (iv) do
not account for the time between the two surgeries and are only suitable for one-stage bilaterals,
and (iii) may introduce bias through the dependence on the particular sample.
problems.locator: Discussion, limitations of landmark analysis and alternative methods

problems.evidence: A survey of seven high-impact journals in the field found 42 percent of clinical studies with multiple observations per patient handling them inappropriately, and the design that produces the bias here was itself a published recommendation. The practice and the critique coexist in the same literature with no marker distinguishing the analyses that carry the assumption.
problems.quote: A review of papers in seven high-impact orthopaedic journals showed that 42% of clinical studies with multiple observations per patient used these multiple observations inappropriately.11

papers.title: Conditioning on future exposure to define study cohorts can induce bias: the case of low-dose acetylsalicylic acid and risk of major bleeding.
papers.one_line: Rebuilds a published continuous-versus-never-user comparison in 6 million Danish adults and shows that defining cohort membership from future prescription redemptions halves the cohort and more than doubles the 90-day risk difference, while leaving the rate ratio almost unchanged.
papers.what_was_done: A cohort study should define membership from current rather than future exposure information, and a published per-protocol-style comparison of continuous versus never use of low-dose acetylsalicylic acid violated that. Two cohorts were built from Danish registries for 2004 to 2011. Cohort 1 used future redemption data to label continuous and never users. Cohort 2 identified initiators and non-initiators from contemporaneous data only and censored follow-up when use changed. Among more than 6 million eligible adults there were 403,693 initiators, of whom 189,150 met the continuous-user definition, so the future-information cohort was less than half the size. Propensity-score-matched Poisson regression gave similar overall incidence rate differences and ratios across cohorts. Stratified by time since initiation the divergence appeared: the 90-day rate difference was 25 per 1,000 person-years in Cohort 1 against 10 in Cohort 2, while the rate ratios stayed close. The paper attributes this to underestimated person-time at risk plus selection on adherence, states the net direction of the two biases is not predictable, and notes that of three ISPE-endorsed guidance documents only the GRACE principles mention immortal time bias and none addresses alignment of eligibility, assignment and follow-up start.

future_research.gap: Methods for adjusting the selection bias that artificial censoring introduces need to be tailored to routinely collected data, where time-varying predictors of adherence are largely unrecorded.
future_research.quote: Future work tailoring these methods for use with routinely collected data (eg, claims data or medical registry data) and their impact on bias reduction is warranted.

future_research.gap: Reporting guidance for database research does not require the timeline showing eligibility, assignment and start of follow-up, and future revisions should add it.
future_research.quote: Future revisions of these guidelines should consider incorporating such information.

problems.evidence: The two cohorts differ only in whether future exposure information was used to assign baseline membership, and that single misalignment more than doubles the early absolute risk. The paper also shows the distortion is scale-dependent, so a study reporting only the ratio would show almost nothing while its absolute risks were wrong by a factor of two and a half.
problems.quote: However, the 90-day IRDs in Cohort 1 were more than double the 90-day IRDs in Cohort 2, likely due to the underestimation of person-time at risk in Cohort 1.

problems.evidence: Three guidance documents endorsed by the same professional society were checked against the specific design failure demonstrated here. One mentions immortal time bias at all and none requires that eligibility, treatment assignment and start of follow-up be aligned, so a study can satisfy the published guidance and still carry the bias the paper measures.
problems.quote: Yet only the GRACE principles include specific consideration of the potential for immortal time bias and none of the guidelines explicitly addresses concerns about alignment of the start of follow-up with treatment assignment and cohort eligibility.

problems.evidence: The design under criticism was an attempt at an observational per-protocol effect, and its failure was to define adherence over the whole follow-up at baseline. The paper states that adherence cannot be randomized, so the target of the original analysis was not a strategy anyone could be assigned to, which is a mismatch between the reported quantity and any assignable estimand.
problems.quote: Such an approach also is not compatible with emulating a hypothetical intervention, which is a prerequisite for causal inference (ie, individuals cannot be randomized to be adherent over a period of time). 27 – 29

problems.evidence: The corrected analysis censors when use changes and therefore needs weights built from time-varying predictors of adherence, which the authors did not build because routine data do not carry them. The censoring correction that the design requires is not available in the data the design is used on.
problems.quote: We did not adjust for factors associated with censoring (eg, via inverse probability weighting), given the general lack of detailed information about time-varying predictors of low-dose ASA adherence.

papers.title: Evaluating beneficial drug effects in a non-interventional setting: a review of effectiveness studies based on Swedish Prescribed Drug Register data.
papers.one_line: Assesses all 24 drug effectiveness studies published from Swedish Prescribed Drug Register data up to 2014 and finds 15 at high risk of bias, one at low risk, two contributing new knowledge, and none guided by a predefined statistical protocol.
papers.what_was_done: Twenty-four effectiveness studies using dispensed-prescription register data were identified from 338 publications of the register's first decade, most on cardiovascular or psychiatric disease. Each was assessed by two clinical pharmacologists against a structured checklist for clinical relevance of the question, risk of bias, and contribution to new knowledge. All had a clinically relevant question. Overall risk of bias was low in one study, moderate in eight and high in fifteen. Two studies were judged to contribute new knowledge on intended drug effects. Recurring failures were selection bias making comparison groups incomparable, treatment bias from suboptimal exposure definition and an intention-to-treat approach imported from trials into a setting where compliance is much lower, and assessment bias including immortal time bias. Good practice observed included propensity score matching and sensitivity analyses. Two studies used propensity score matching, both cardiovascular. Quality registers gave better clinical variables but excluded large fractions of patients through incompleteness. No publication reported being guided by a predefined protocol specifying the statistical analyses and a clinically meaningful difference. The review notes it likely reflects the better subset, since unpublished and reimbursement-application analyses do not undergo peer review.

future_research.gap: Expectations of what register-based effectiveness evidence can deliver to decision makers need to be lowered until the methodological problems are addressed.
future_research.quote: Although this review illustrates that effectiveness studies based on dispensed drug register data can contribute to new evidence of intended effects of drug treatment in clinical practice, the expectations of such data to provide valuable information need to be tempered due to methodological issues.

problems.evidence: Across every study in a complete decade of output from one national register, not one stated that its statistical analysis was fixed in advance. The analytic protocol was therefore available for revision after the data were seen in all 24 studies, and the review classes this as a pitfall that is relatively easy to handle, meaning the absence is a convention rather than a constraint.
problems.quote: Another pitfall, which is relatively easy to handle, was that no publication in this review stated that it was guided by a predefined protocol describing the statistical analyses and defining the size of a clinically meaningful difference between the comparison groups.

problems.evidence: Two of 24 studies were judged to contribute new knowledge, and the judgment is a binary verdict from a structured checklist rather than a calibrated comparison against what was already established. The review reports its inter-rater agreement as good but gives no scale on which a near miss and a clear failure differ.
problems.quote: According to the systematic quality assessments, the overall risk of bias was low in one (4%), moderate in eight (33%) and high in 15 (62%) studies. Overall, two (8%) studies were assessed as contributing to new knowledge.

problems.evidence: The review states the data-fitness requirement as coverage plus the relevant variables, and shows it failing in practice: some studies using quality registers excluded a large proportion of patients for incompleteness, and administrative databases with dispensations and diagnoses may not carry essential clinical data. No threshold is given at which either shortfall should stop a study.
problems.quote: Indeed, to provide adequate evidence, justifying the efforts in health care to collect the data, registers need to have both acceptable coverage and a set‐up including the relevant variables.

problems.evidence: Almost half the studies adopted an intention-to-treat approach carried over from trials, where its conservatism is accepted because adherence is monitored. The review argues that with practice-level compliance the misclassification is much larger, so the quantity being reported is not the conservative version of the intended effect that the label implies.
problems.quote: Consequently, the intention‐to‐treat approach may be less appropriate in this setting.

papers.title: Metformin and cancer in type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and comprehensive bias evaluation.
papers.one_line: Rates all 46 observational studies of metformin and cancer against eight prespecified bias domains, finds three clean in every domain, and shows the strongest protective estimates come from the studies with the highest total bias score.
papers.what_was_done: MEDLINE was searched for observational studies of metformin and overall or site-specific cancer in type 2 diabetes. Each of 46 studies was rated unlikely, low, medium or high against eight domains fixed in advance: outcome, exposure, control selection, baseline confounding, time-dependent confounding, immortal time, missing data and censoring methods. Twenty-one studies assessed all cancer, with relative risks from 0.23 to 1.22; twelve reported a statistically significant protective effect and none a harmful one. Three of 46 studies were low or unlikely in every domain, two of which were consistent with no effect and the third reporting a modest protective estimate for long-term use, hazard ratio 0.82 with interval 0.75 to 0.90, that its own authors judged inconsistent with causality. Twenty-eight studies were at risk through exposure definition, 22 through insufficient baseline adjustment and 35 through time-dependent confounding. Summing domain scores gave a total bias score; heterogeneity rose with that score and the strongest protective effects sat at the high end. Directed acyclic graphs show what three common adjustment approaches actually estimate: adjusting for a mid-follow-up HbA1c blocks the mediated effect, adjusting once at baseline with time-varying exposure leaves residual confounding, and fixing exposure at baseline gives an intention-to-treat quantity only.

future_research.gap: Because the studies at low risk of other biases all handled time-dependent confounding the same way, the existing literature cannot say whether time-dependent confounding affected by prior treatment matters for this question.
future_research.quote: The lack of variation in how time-dependent confounders were adjusted for in these studies mean that it is not possible with the current literature alone to assess whether there is a meaningful impact of time-dependent confounders affected by previous treatment on the estimated effect of metformin on cancer risk.

future_research.gap: Marginal structural models or the g-formula have not been applied to this question and would be a valuable addition.
future_research.quote: Causal methodology has been successfully used in other areas to overcome issues with time-dependent confounders affected by previous treatment,

problems.evidence: Across 46 studies of one exposure-outcome pair there is no variation in estimator for the hardest part of the problem, so the literature contains no evidence about whether the choice mattered. The three approaches that were used are shown by directed acyclic graphs to target three different quantities, yet all are reported as the effect of metformin on cancer.
problems.quote: Most studies with low risk of other biases used the approach outlines in 5D.

problems.evidence: The review's central empirical result is that heterogeneity in estimates tracks a summed bias score and the largest protective effects sit at the high end. This is a calibrated comparison rather than a binary pass, and it is offered as a bias evaluation rather than as a replication standard, so nothing carries the method to a new question.
problems.quote: When ordered by this score [ Figure 4 (right)] it is clear that heterogeneity increases as risk of bias increases, and the strongest protective effects are from those studies with the highest risk of bias overall.

problems.evidence: Exposure definition was the single largest bias domain, affecting 28 of 46 studies, and the paper shows that estimates within the low-risk group move toward the null. What counts as being on metformin, over what window and with what allowance for switching, is the operative decision, and no procedure fixes it.
problems.quote: However, 28/46 studies were at risk from bias through exposure definition, 22 through insufficient baseline adjustment and 35 from possible time-dependent confounding.

problems.evidence: Fixing exposure at cohort entry removes time-dependent confounding at the cost of estimating an intention-to-treat quantity, which the paper states is questionable when patients do not stay on one treatment. The studies using this approach are the ones judged at low risk of other biases, so the cleanest studies in the review are reporting a different estimand from the pharmacological effect the review set out to assess.
problems.quote: In Figure 5D , the fixing of exposure from baseline removes the issue of time-dependent confounding and therefore allows the total effect of exposure on cancer to be estimated, but typically estimates an ITT effect only, which may not be appropriate given that patients are unlikely to adhere to a single treatment throughout follow-up.

papers.title: Risk of Preterm or Small-for-Gestational-Age Birth After Influenza Vaccination During Pregnancy: Caveats When Conducting Retrospective Observational Studies.
papers.one_line: In 46,549 Vaccine Safety Datalink pregnancies, a strong protective association between H1N1 vaccination and preterm birth disappears once vaccine access, seasonality and immortal time are handled, while the same treatment leaves the small-for-gestational-age result unchanged.
papers.what_was_done: Pregnant women are excluded from prelicensure trials, so postmarketing safety assessment falls to observational data. Across eight Vaccine Safety Datalink sites, 46,549 pregnancies during 2009 to 2010 were analyzed, 40 percent with monovalent H1N1 vaccine, for preterm birth under 37 weeks and small-for-gestational-age birth. Three sources of bias were identified and handled: variable access to vaccine over the campaign period, which meant only women already further along could be vaccinated in its early weeks; seasonal confounding from pregnancy start date; and the time-dependent nature of vaccination within pregnancy. Ignoring these gave a relative risk of 0.79 with interval 0.74 to 0.85. Handling them gave 0.91 with interval 0.83 to 1.0. The small-for-gestational-age association showed no important bias from the same sources, consistent with its definition being independent of gestational age. Only calendar date of last menstrual period drove the propensity score, indicating little confounding by indication. Adding H1N1 circulation as a time-dependent covariate did not change results. The review of prior work found several studies lacking or incompletely capturing vaccination date, and only a few using a time-dependent covariate method.

future_research.gap: Whether excluding stillbirths distorts the association between maternal vaccination and birth outcomes could not be evaluated because the analysis was restricted to livebirths.
future_research.quote:
Finally, our analyses
were restricted to livebirths, and thus we were unable to evaluate
whether the exclusion of stillbirth affected the observed maternal MIV–birth outcome associations.

problems.evidence: The entire apparent benefit is produced by design choices about time, and the paper shows that the conventional confounding toolkit does not reach them. Access to vaccination, seasonality and immortal time are three separate time-structural problems that a propensity score cannot address, and the paper's own list of prior studies shows most did not address all three.
problems.quote:
For example, focusing on conventional methods, such as multivariable adjustment, propensity methods, matching, or exclusion of women
who have rare exposure to risk factors, may not be sufﬁcient
to address other potential biases, such as access to vaccination,
seasonal confounding, and immortal time bias.

problems.evidence: Eligibility required continuous insurance coverage and at least one outpatient encounter, both healthcare-use variables, and the cohort further excluded pregnancies with no recorded birth outcome. Each condition selects on contact with the system that also determines whether vaccination is recorded, and the paper reports the resulting under-representation without analyzing what it does to the estimate.
problems.quote: Our cohort was limited to women with continuous insurance coverage and at least 1 outpatient encounter.

problems.evidence: The survey of prior studies shows the field split on whether vaccination timing was captured at all, with some studies lacking the date, some capturing it incompletely and some relying on self-report, and only a few using time-dependent methods. The published estimates carry different assumption burdens and are reported in a common format that does not distinguish them.
problems.quote:
Several studies lacked the date of vaccination (3, 4), had incomplete capture of vaccination date (8, 42),
or used self-reported data (5, 19).

papers.title: Invited Commentary: Influenza, Influenza Immunization, and Pregnancy-It's About Time.
papers.one_line: Sets out why an anytime-in-pregnancy exposure definition creates immortal time whose size scales with how early the outcome occurs, and states a data-availability condition under which studies of fetal benefit from maternal immunization should not be attempted at all.
papers.what_was_done: Two studies in the same issue found no association between circulating influenza and adverse pregnancy outcomes, and showed that an apparent protective effect of immunization on preterm birth largely disappears under appropriate methodology. The commentary explains the temporal structure that produces this. Classifying a pregnancy as vaccinated if vaccination occurred at any point creates immortal time, because a pregnancy that ends early has less opportunity to be vaccinated, which inflates the denominator of the preterm birth rate among the vaccinated. Accounting for immortal time moved the risk ratio from 0.79 with interval 0.74 to 0.85 to 0.88 with interval 0.82 to 0.94, while further adjustment for confounding moved it only from 0.91 to 0.92, so the time-related bias exceeded confounding. The effect was largest in the third trimester, risk ratio 0.63, and absent for small-for-gestational-age birth, which is defined independently of gestational age. Continuing follow-up past the window in which an outcome can occur has the opposite consequence. The recommended framework uses gestational days rather than pregnancies as the unit, restricts follow-up to the period at risk, classifies exposure time-varyingly with pre-vaccination time unexposed, and treats calendar-time influenza circulation as an effect modifier rather than a time-dependent covariate.

future_research.gap: Whether influenza illness acts within a critical gestational window is unknown, and until it is, analysis plans cannot target the right time interval.
future_research.quote:
Although it is unknown whether there is a critical time
window during which inﬂuenza illness exerts its effect on
fetal health, an analysis plan that fails to allow for narrower
time windows of effect reduces the potential to detect harm
from inﬂuenza illness or beneﬁts from immunization.

future_research.gap: Outcomes occurring at earlier gestational ages than preterm birth are expected to carry more immortal time bias, which has not been quantified.
future_research.quote:
We speculate that outcomes that occur at systematically younger
gestational ages than preterm births (such as stillbirth and infant
death) will have an even greater degree of bias because of immortal time.

problems.evidence: The size of the bias is set by where follow-up starts and stops relative to the interval in which the outcome can occur, and the commentary shows both errors in the same setting: including gestational time after 37 weeks in a preterm birth study, and letting exposure accumulate over a whole pregnancy. Neither boundary is derivable from the exposure or the data; both come from knowing the outcome's biology.
problems.quote:
Immortal time bias is introduced by an “anytime-in-pregnancy” exposure definition because
the shortened pregnancy duration associated with many adverse fetal outcomes limits the opportunity to become
exposed, whereas including follow-up time during which pregnancies are no longer at risk of an adverse outcome
(e.g., gestational time after 37 weeks in studies of preterm birth) can lead to overestimation of any true benefits of
immunization (or harms from influenza illness).

problems.evidence: This is a data-fitness criterion of the kind usually missing: it names two specific variables, the calendar time of viral circulation and the gestational age at vaccination, and states that without them the study should not be undertaken. It is stated for one exposure and one outcome family and derived from the biology rather than from a general procedure, so it does not generalize on its own.
problems.quote:
We present a framework to avoid time-related biases in the study
of influenza illness and immunization in pregnancy and advise that investigations of fetal benefit from maternal influenza immunization should only be undertaken when information is available on the calendar time of influenza virus
circulation and the gestational age at which maternal influenza immunization occurred.

problems.evidence: Adjusting for viral circulation as a time-dependent covariate returns a weighted average over seasons in which the vaccine can and cannot work, which is not the effect anyone intended to estimate. The distinction between a covariate and an effect modifier decides which estimand comes out, and both analyses would be reported as the effect of immunization.
problems.quote:
Controlling for inﬂuenza virus circulation as a time-dependent
covariate is not appropriate because doing so will produce an
estimate of effect that is the weighted average of the vaccine’s
effects during the inﬂuenza season and noninﬂuenza season.

problems.evidence: An exposure defined as occurring at any point in pregnancy adds exposure in periods irrelevant to etiology to exposure in the periods that matter, which is misclassification that biases toward the null for gestational-age-dependent outcomes. The exposure variable is binary and recorded without error, and the error is entirely in what the binary variable is taken to mean.
problems.quote:
Exposures such as this are particularly prone to misclassiﬁcation when an “anytime-duringpregnancy” exposure deﬁnition is used with an agent that
only exerts its effects in a limited period of development (19),
adding inconsequential exposure to exposure in the time periods
that are relevant to disease etiology.

papers.title: Specifying a target trial prevents immortal time bias and other self-inflicted injuries in observational analyses.
papers.one_line: States the alignment principle that eligibility, treatment assignment and start of follow-up must coincide, gives randomization and cloning as the two valid ways to assign individuals whose baseline data do not determine a strategy, and marks the boundary of what alignment buys.
papers.what_was_done: An observational analysis is treated as an attempt to emulate a target trial, and the biases addressed here are those that arise not from missing confounders but from departing from principles that govern trial design. The central principle is that time zero is the moment when eligibility is met and a treatment strategy is assigned. Four justifications researchers give for breaking this alignment are examined in turn. One is that baseline data may not determine which strategy an individual's data are consistent with, which arises for dynamic strategies such as initiate therapy if hemoglobin drops below 10 g/dL, because everyone has hemoglobin above the threshold at time zero. Using later information to classify individuals misaligns eligibility and assignment; the two valid alternatives are random assignment to a strategy or cloning, each requiring variance adjustment. Both make the intention-to-treat analogue inestimable, because the same individuals or exchangeable groups populate every strategy, so only a per-protocol analogue with censoring at deviation and weighting for the induced selection remains. The paper is explicit that alignment does not deliver correct emulation on its own.

problems.evidence: The alignment principle removes immortal time by construction and is the foundation the rest of the field builds on. What it does not supply is any rule for the grid on which time zero and subsequent decisions are placed, or for how long a grace period may run before the data stop being consistent with a strategy; the paper takes the strategies and their timing as given.
problems.quote:
One of those principles is the specification of time zero of follow-up as the
time when the eligibility criteria are met and a treatment
strategy is assigned.

problems.evidence: Cloning is introduced here as the remedy for indeterminate baseline assignment, and the paper states its consequence: because the same individual populates every strategy, the incidence rate is equal across strategies by construction and the intention-to-treat analogue cannot be estimated. What remains is a per-protocol quantity conditional on the censoring model, so cloning changes what is estimable rather than only how it is estimated.
problems.quote: The observational analog of the intention-to-treat effect cannot be estimated.

problems.evidence: The paper's own conclusion states that synchronizing eligibility, assignment and time zero does not make an emulation correct, and that confounding and other biases still make the inference suspect. Specifying a target trial is a discipline that removes one class of self-inflicted error; it carries no information about the assumption burden that remains.
problems.quote:
The synchronization of eligibility, treatment assignment,
and time zero does not ensure that the observational analyses will correctly emulate the target trial.

problems.evidence: Insufficient confounder information is named at the outset as the most prominent reason an emulation fails, and it is then set aside as outside the scope of the alignment framework. The paper offers nothing that would detect or bound it, and the closing statement is that causal inference from these data remains suspect even under perfect synchronization.
problems.quote: Most prominently, the observational data may contain insufficient information on confounders to approximately emulate randomization [2].
